topics.label: Introduction to inflammation initiation and resolution
topics.groupedBecause: This opening frames the lecture as an integration of previously introduced immune cells and molecules.

topics.label: Principles of innate immune recognition
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how germline-encoded receptors distinguish microbial products and tissue damage from normal host components.

topics.label: Toll-like receptor recognition and signalling
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how toll-like receptors translate microbial recognition into responses shaped by the location of detection.

topics.label: Other pattern recognition receptors and inflammasome activation
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics develop recognition pathways beyond toll-like receptors that connect infection or damage sensing to inflammatory disease.

topics.label: Sentinel-cell activation and inflammatory cell recruitment
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics trace how activated sentinel cells generate inflammatory signals that mobilize immune cells to an infection site.

topics.label: Lymphatic transport and adaptive immune priming
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic explains how drainage from infected tissues carries evidence of infection to lymph nodes for adaptive immune activation.

topics.label: Excessive systemic inflammation and septic shock
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic examines how excessive inflammatory activation produces dangerous systemic effects and septic shock.

topics.label: Passive and active resolution of inflammation
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic explains how inflammatory responses are shut down through declining stimulation and active inhibitory signals.

topics.label: Tissue repair and persistent inflammation
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics examine why inflamed tissue may fail to return to normal and how persistent inflammation can sometimes contain an otherwise uncleared infection.

topics.label: Lecture close and next lecture on complement
topics.groupedBecause: This closing ends the lecture and identifies complement as the subject of the next lecture.
